title: The slot system standard — single register, four props shares, and the framework store seat
summary: The browser page is composed at run time from plugins through one slot registry: only the root slot exists up front, and a plugin registers into a slot, declares its child slots and its store, and supplies pure React components whose props are derived from four sources.
firstReason: The need (features contribute UI into named regions owned by a parent) stands, but with server-rendered HTML it becomes named template regions that Go components fill on the server; React props, stores and hooks do not exist.

title: Client plugin loading — lazy factories, Cordis lifecycle, and hot reload
summary: The browser runs the same plugin mechanism as the host: a client module system loads lazy plugin factories, the plugin loader governs their lifecycle, and changed plugins are hot-reloaded in the page.
firstReason: The Go design has no JavaScript plugin runtime in the browser; UI contributions are rendered by server components, and a change reaches the page by re-rendering, not by reloading modules.

title: One carrier-level browser-trust boundary for all `/api` routes
summary: Browser trust is enforced once for the whole /api prefix: every POST must declare application/json, and every request must present a Host that is loopback or explicitly trusted, with any Origin matching it. This blocks cross-site simple requests and DNS rebinding against the local API.
firstReason: A local HTTP API that can run shell commands needs these two fences whatever the server language; in Go they become one middleware in front of every route, including the htmx and server-sent-event routes.

title: Client shell layering and dynamic package boundaries
summary: The browser application is layered into a compilation shell, a framework-free startup kernel, static shared libraries and dynamically loaded client packages, with explicit rules for what each may bundle or import.
firstReason: These layers exist to control what a JavaScript bundler inlines and which module instances are shared. With server-rendered HTML there is one shell template and a few self-contained script islands, so the layering has no counterpart.

title: Client Session, Conversation, and UI ownership layers
summary: The web client is layered as controller and domain object, then UI adapter, then renderer, then slot component; domain objects publish React-free observable sources and components read only from slot props.
firstReason: The ownership idea (domain state is separate from presentation) is kept, but the layers collapse: the Go host holds the domain state and renders templates from it, so there are no observable sources, adapters or hooks in the browser.

title: Locale-owned client UI copy
summary: All product-authored wording in the client comes from typed locale dictionaries; data authored by users, models or providers is shown verbatim, and shared UI primitives receive their text as required props with no built-in language fallback.
firstReason: The rule (product text comes from a catalogue, data is never translated) is kept, but the catalogue is read by Go templates on the server instead of being passed as typed React props.

title: Client resource model
summary: Anything a UI component reads live is a resource identified only by a dsh-resource address; the address's protocol names the one provider that streams it, and components share one copy through a useResource hook.
firstReason: Addressable, shared live data is still wanted, but in the Go design an address maps to a server route that renders a fragment and a server-sent-event stream that updates it; the hook and the client cache disappear.

title: Reusable component factories with local slots
summary: Beside ordinary slots, a package can register a reusable component factory that any parent may render several times, each parent choosing the components for the factory's local slots.
firstReason: Reusable UI assemblies with caller-chosen parts become Go template partials that take named blocks; the React factory registry is not needed.

title: Semantic phases for composer-chain election
summary: Proposal (not built upstream): the composer area chooses what to show by named phases (a pending question or approval first, a read-only restriction second) instead of one global numeric priority.
firstReason: Adopt the rule that resolving a pending interaction outranks a restriction, but implement it where the Go host selects the composer template; the client slot chain does not exist.

title: Window drag coverage as a contract
summary: On the macOS desktop app, which parts of the window can be dragged is declared once: each chrome row marks itself in markup, one CSS rule makes marked rows draggable, and tests run an executable model of the drag-region rule against a manifest of rows.
firstReason: The duplication it removes came from React packages each hand-writing drag regions. With server-rendered templates there is one shell layout, so the single-declaration goal is met by construction; the Go desktop shell has its own drag-region convention that the desktop spec must name.

title: Keep shortcut preferences device-local and commit before activation
summary: Keyboard shortcut overrides are stored per device (browser storage on the web, a shell-owned file on desktop), not in the host. A new binding takes effect only after it was saved, and unreadable or newer-version preference data is never overwritten.
firstReason: One host serves several devices with different operating systems and browser restrictions, so bindings cannot be host state. Commit-before-activate and never-overwrite-unreadable are storage rules that hold for the Go desktop shell and the browser island alike.

title: Client plugin package assets served by URL
summary: A client plugin package ships its images as files served under `/plugins/<package>/assets/` with a content hash in the file name, instead of embedding them as base64 in the JavaScript bundle.
firstReason: There is no client plugin bundle in the Go design. Inference: first-party assets are embedded in the binary and served with content-hashed names; how a plugin process contributes static assets is for the plugin protocol to define.

title: Add the `hoc` slot kind so plugins can wrap owner content in layers
summary: The client slot system gains a fifth kind, `hoc`, that lets a plugin wrap the owner's content in ordered layers and so become an ancestor of that content, which the sibling-only slot kinds cannot do.
firstReason: The need (an extension decorates or wraps a region it does not own) stands, but a React higher-order component has no meaning in server-rendered HTML. The Go UI needs a template-level wrapper extension point with the same ordering and shadowing rules.

title: Client metadata and renderer-owned stylesheet installation
summary: A client module artifact carries optional metadata that describes its stylesheets by path. The module system owns JavaScript identity, and the renderer installs, de-duplicates, updates and removes stylesheets in the main document; script loading no longer injects CSS.
firstReason: The goal (a stylesheet reaches the page once and its lifetime belongs to the document, not to script loading) stands. The Go host serves stylesheets as static assets linked from templates, so there are no client module manifests to carry them.

title: Authentication Provider integration
summary: Shows how a credential plugin plugs in: it uses the `connection` service to create a Peer (the authenticated caller identity) and the nested `connection.authentication` service to register a verifier. Route owners and transports receive the selected Peer and never handle tokens.
firstReason: Keeping credential knowledge out of transports and route handlers is a security boundary, not a JavaScript artefact. In Go the provider is an interface registered with an authentication service and the Peer travels in the request context.

title: Peer-based authentication Providers
summary: Authentication is an independent service that tries registered credential Providers in registration order and accepts the first live Peer. If all refuse the answer is 401, and if a verifier failed it is 503; the web server enforces route admission, and gateway and remote access authorize operations from the Peer.
firstReason: The host serves tool-capable operations, so a reachable address must never establish identity, and one authorization model for browser token, desktop and remote pairing is needed whatever the UI technology. Server-rendered pages and server-sent event streams pass through the same admission.

title: Browser plugin configuration sync
summary: Browser plugins receive the volatile (live-updatable) fields of their host configuration, pushed on change without remounting the plugin. Secret positions are removed on the host and never sent, and equal values cause no update.
firstReason: The goal (a configuration change shows in an open page without a reload, and secrets never leave the host) stands. With server-rendered HTML there is no browser plugin to configure: the host renders from current configuration and pushes re-rendered fragments over server-sent events.

title: Generic file upload
summary: Non-image files are uploaded in the background through one FIFO queue as soon as they are picked, stored byte for byte with no type or size limit, and staged for the session under a receipt. Equal bytes are stored once under their digest, and each model-facing path is a read-only hard link to that object.
firstReason: Content-addressed storage with hard-linked names and receipt-based staging is host-side and language-neutral. The browser upload carriers become an ordinary HTTP upload from the Go UI.

title: Prompt to reload when the Host release changes instead of hot-replacing across releases
summary: A release is the host's version plus an optional source commit. A page applies hot module updates only while the connected host serves the release the page booted from; when the release differs, nothing is applied and a dialog asks the user to reload.
firstReason: A page left open across a host upgrade still happens with server-rendered HTML, because the scripts and styles it loaded belong to the old release. The Go UI has no module graph to hot-replace, so the mechanism reduces to comparing a release identity on reconnect and prompting for a reload.

title: Composer image upload on add
summary: The composer uploads each image as soon as it is added, through the same background queue as files. The host validates, normalizes and stores it and returns a receipt; the prompt cites the receipt, and stored images count toward the per-message limits.
firstReason: Sending a message no longer carries megabytes of base64 in one call, and validation errors appear when the image is added. Receipt-based staging is host-side and suits an HTML upload.

title: Migrate existing browser configuration reads to configuration sync
summary: Proposal, not built upstream: an inventory of packages whose browser half reads host configuration by its own means (page globals, the settings mirror) and a plan to move each of them to browser configuration sync.
firstReason: Do not adopt. The plan migrates React client code that DH-ADR-3 replaces; a server-rendered page reads host configuration when it renders, so there is nothing to migrate. The inventory remains useful as a list of UI features that depend on host configuration.

title: Task Surface for structured session interaction
summary: Proposal, not built upstream: Task Surface, a versioned declarative description of a temporary structured interaction (compare options, reorder a plan, fill related fields) that an agent emits for one tool call. The product validates, places and renders it and returns the user's conclusion; no generated code runs.
firstReason: Adopt the idea with a different renderer. A bounded declarative model is easier to serve from a Go host than from a client plugin: the host validates the description and renders it with templates, which DH-ADR-3 already requires.
